case_results.question: What are the essential requirements for anticipatory bail under Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023?
case_results.answer_text:
The essential requirements for anticipatory bail under Section 482 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are as follows:

1. The person must have reason to believe that they may be arrested on an accusation of having committed a non-bailable offence [Section 482(1)].
2. The person must apply to the High Court or the Court of Session for a direction under Section 482 [Section 482(1)].
3. The High Court or the Court of Session may, if it thinks fit, direct that in the event of such arrest, the person shall be released on bail [Section 482(1)].
4. The Court may include conditions in the direction for bail, such as:
   - A condition that the person shall make themselves available for interrogation by a police officer as and when required [Section 482(2)(i)].
   - A condition that the person shall not, directly or indirectly, make any inducement, threat, or promise to any person acquainted with the facts of the case so as to dissuade them from disclosing such facts to the Court or to any police officer [Section 482(2)(ii)].
   - A condition that the person shall not leave India without the previous permission of the Court [Section 482(2)(iii)].
   - Such other conditions as may be imposed under sub-section (3) of section 480 [Section 482(2)(iv)].

It is essential to note that Section 482 does not apply to cases involving the arrest of any person on accusation of having committed an offence under section 65 and sub-section (2) of section 70 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 [Section 482(4)].

Additionally, the Court may refuse to release a person on bail if they have failed to comply with the conditions of the bond or bail bond as regards the time and place of attendance [Section 478(2)].

The bond or bail bond must be executed by the person and, when released on bail, by one or more sufficient sureties, conditioned that the person shall attend at the time and place mentioned in the bond, and shall continue so to attend until otherwise directed by the police officer or Court [Section 485(1)].

The bond or bail bond may also contain conditions imposed for the release of the person on bail, such as appearing when called upon at the High Court, Court of Session, or other Court to answer the charge [Section 485(3)].

Finally, the Court may require the accused to execute a bond or bail bond to appear before the higher Court as and when such Court issues notice in respect of any appeal or petition filed against the judgment of the respective Court [Section 481(1)].

case_results.question: What are the grounds for eviction of a tenant under Section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958?
case_results.answer_text:
The grounds for eviction of a tenant under Section 14 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, are specified in the proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 14. According to Section 14(1) of the Act, the Controller may make an order for the recovery of the possession of the premises on one or more of the following grounds only:

1. The tenant has neither paid nor tendered the whole of the arrears of the rent legally recoverable from him within two months of the date on which a notice of demand for the arrears of rent has been served on him by the landlord in the manner provided in section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. [Section 14(1)(a) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958]

2. The tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord. [Section 14(1)(b) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958]

3. The premises let for residential purposes are required bona fide by the landlord for occupation as a residence for himself or for any member of his family dependent on him, if he is the owner thereof, or for any person for whose benefit the premises are held and that the landlord or such person has no other reasonably suitable residential accommodation. [Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958]

However, it is essential to note that the Supreme Court, in the case of Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another, has held that the words 'let for residential purposes' in Section 14(1)(e) are unconstitutional and have been severed. This means that landlords can now seek eviction for commercial bona fide requirement as well. [Satyawati Sharma (Dead) by LRs v. Union of India and Another, Para 1]

In addition, Section 25B of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, provides a special procedure for the disposal of applications for eviction on the ground of bona fide requirement. According to this section, the tenant on whom the summons is duly served shall not contest the prayer for eviction from the premises unless he files an affidavit stating the grounds on which he seeks to contest the application for eviction and obtains leave from the Controller. [Section 25B(4) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958]

The term 'landlord' is defined in Section 2(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, as a person who, for the time being, is receiving, or is entitled to receive, the rent of any premises. [Section 2(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958]

The term 'tenant' is defined in Section 2(l) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, as any person by whom or on whose account or behalf the rent of any premises is, or, but for a special contract, would be, payable, and includes a sub-tenant and also any person continuing in possession after the termination of his tenancy. [Section 2(l) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958]

1. **Admissibility of electronic records**: Section 61 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 states that nothing in this Adhiniyam shall apply to deny the admissibility of an electronic or digital record in the evidence on the ground that it is an electronic or digital record [Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 61]. Such records shall have the same legal effect, validity, and enforceability as other documents, subject to the provisions of section 63 [Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 61].

2. **Certificate requirement**: Where any electronic record is produced in evidence, it shall be accompanied by a certificate referred to in sub-section (4) of section 63 [Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 61, Proviso 1].

3. **Definition of electronic records**: For the purposes of this section, an electronic or digital record includes records stored, generated, received, or sent in an electronic form or micro-films, computer-generated fiche, and any other form as defined in clause (t) of sub-section (1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 [Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, Section 61, Explanation].

4. **Section 63**: The provisions of section 63 are relevant to the admissibility of electronic records, but the specific text of section 63 is not provided in the retrieved evidence passages.

5. **Jurisdiction**: The Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 61, states that no court shall have jurisdiction to entertain any suit or proceeding in respect of any matter which an adjudicating officer appointed under this Act or the Appellate Tribunal constituted under this Act is empowered by or under this Act to determine [The Information Technology Act, 2000, Section 61]. However, this provision is not directly related to the admissibility of electronic records under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.

In conclusion, the admissibility of electronic records under Section 61 and Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 is governed by the provisions of Section 61, which states that electronic records shall have the same legal effect, validity, and enforceability as other documents, subject to the provisions of section 63. The certificate requirement and definition of electronic records are also specified in Section 61.

case_results.question: What constitutes cheque bouncing under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881?
case_results.answer_text:
Cheque bouncing under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, is constituted by the following conditions:

1. The cheque must be drawn by a person on an account maintained by them with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability [The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 138].
2. The cheque must be returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank [The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 138].
3. The cheque must be presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier [The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 138 Proviso 1].
4. The payee or holder in due course of the cheque must make a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid [The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 138 Proviso 2].
5. The drawer of such cheque must fail to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice [The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 138 Proviso 3].

Additionally, the Explanation to Section 138 clarifies that for the purposes of this section, 'debt or other liability' means a legally enforceable debt or other liability [The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 138 Explanation].

case_results.question: What is the doctrine of frustration of contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872?
case_results.answer_text:
The doctrine of frustration of contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, is a concept that renders a contract void when an act becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made. This is explicitly stated in Evidence Item 1, which reads:

"A contract to do an act which, after the contract is made, becomes impossible, or, by reason of some event which the promisor could not prevent, unlawful, becomes void when the act becomes impossible or unlawful." [The Indian Contract Act, 1872, Section 56]

This provision makes it clear that if a contract is entered into to perform an act that becomes impossible or unlawful after the contract is made, the contract becomes void. The provision does not leave the matter to the intention of the parties or English common law implied term doctrines, as held in the Supreme Court judgment of Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another [1953-09-16], which states:

"Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act lays down a positive rule of law relating to frustration and does not leave the matter to the intention of the parties or English common law implied term doctrines." [Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another, Holding 1]

It is essential to note that the other evidence passages provided do not directly relate to the doctrine of frustration of contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Evidence Item 2 refers to a section of the Information Technology Act, 2000, which has been omitted, and Evidence Item 3 refers to a section of the Maharashtra Police Act, 1951, which deals with the removal of persons about to commit an offence. Evidence Item 4 refers to a section of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which deals with the health and safety of an arrested person.

Therefore, the doctrine of frustration of contract under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, is governed by the provisions of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, and the Supreme Court judgment of Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Another.

case_results.question: What is the binding rule regarding mandatory certificates for electronic evidence as laid down in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020)?
case_results.answer_text:
The binding rule regarding mandatory certificates for electronic evidence, as laid down in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020), is as follows:

1. A Section 65B(4) / Section 63(4) certificate is mandatory for secondary electronic evidence [EVIDENCE ITEM 1: Holding 1, Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal and Others (2020)].
2. Oral evidence in the place of such certificate cannot suffice [EVIDENCE ITEM 1: Holding 1, Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal and Others (2020)].
3. The certificate under sub-section (4) is a condition precedent to the admissibility of evidence by way of electronic record [EVIDENCE ITEM 2: Paragraph 51, Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal and Others (2020)].
4. However, the requirement of producing a certificate under Section 65B(4) is not always mandatory and can be relaxed whenever the interest of justice so warrants, particularly where the party is not in possession of the device [EVIDENCE ITEM 5: Holding 1, Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2018)].

It is essential to note that the Supreme Court has overruled the earlier judgment in Shafhi Mohammad v. State of Himachal Pradesh (2018) in Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) 7 SCC 1, making the certificate under Section 65B(4) mandatory for secondary electronic evidence.

Therefore, the binding rule is that a Section 65B(4) / Section 63(4) certificate is mandatory for secondary electronic evidence, and oral evidence in the place of such certificate cannot suffice. However, the requirement of producing a certificate under Section 65B(4) can be relaxed in exceptional cases where the party is not in possession of the device and the interest of justice so warrants.

case_results.question: What guidelines did the Supreme Court establish in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI regarding arrest and bail categorization?
case_results.answer_text:
The Supreme Court established the following guidelines in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI regarding arrest and bail categorization:

1. **Bail is the rule and jail is the exception**: This principle has been reiterated by the Supreme Court, emphasizing the importance of personal liberty under Article 21 of the Constitution. [Paragraph 73]

2. **Non-compliance with Section 41 and 41A CrPC entitles the accused to bail as of right**: The Supreme Court held that any arrest made in violation of the mandate under Section 41 and 41A will entitle the accused to grant of bail. [Paragraph 26]

3. **Category A offences (punishable with imprisonment of 7 years or less) require issuance of summons in the first instance**: After filing of chargesheet, summons should ordinarily be issued in the first instance for Category A offences. If the accused was not arrested during investigation, bail application may be decided without insisting upon custodial detention. [Paragraph 100]

4. **Arrest is a draconian power that cannot be exercised mechanically**: The Supreme Court emphasized that arrest should not be exercised mechanically, and when an accused person is not arrested during investigation and cooperates with the police pursuant to notice under Section 41A CrPC, the court should decide bail applications on the same day or without custodial remand. [Ratio Decidendi]

5. **Compliance with Section 41 and 41A of the Code is mandatory**: The Supreme Court held that Section 41 and 41A of the Code are salutary provisions, and compliance thereof is mandatory. A court, while considering the application for custody or remand under Section 167 of the Code, is duty-bound to satisfy itself that the mandate of Section 41 and 41A has been strictly adhered to. [Paragraph 26]

These guidelines are binding across India under Article 141 of the Constitution, as per the Supreme Court's judgment in Satender Kumar Antil v. CBI.

The decision in NN Global (2023) 7 SCC 1 and SMS Tea Estates (2011) 14 SCC 66 stand overruled [Evidence Item 4, Paragraph 224(d)]. The principle of competence-competence, enshrined in Section 16 of the Arbitration Act, empowers the arbitral tribunal to rule on its own jurisdiction, including ruling on any objections with respect to the existence or validity of the arbitration agreement [Evidence Item 3, Paragraph 175].

At the referral stage under Section 8 or Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, the court must only examine the prima facie existence of the arbitration agreement, leaving questions of stamping and admissibility to the arbitral tribunal under Section 16 [Evidence Item 5, Ratio Decidendi].

Therefore, the 7-Judge Constitution Bench in Re Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements and the Stamp Act has indeed overruled NN Global Mercantile (2023) [Evidence Item 4, Paragraph 224].
